text: A report page should make exactly one point clearly at a glance, not show off every chart type you happen to know how to build. Here's how to keep that point honest while you're at it, because a handful of common choices genuinely mislead readers.

Three-D effects and axes that don't start at zero both exaggerate differences between values, making a small gap look dramatic. Pie, donut, and gauge charts lose their point past a small number of slices — the human brain compares bar lengths far more accurately than it compares angles or areas, so keep pie charts under roughly eight categories. And mixing a measure in the millions with one in the thousands on the same axis flattens the smaller series completely, even if it's actually moving significantly — reach for a second axis or a combo chart instead.

Keep displayed numbers to three or four significant digits — three point four million reads faster and more accurately than the full number spelled out digit by digit. And sorting isn't just tidiness, it's a genuine storytelling decision: sort by the measure to highlight the highest or lowest value, or sort by category when you want a viewer to quickly locate one specific item among many. Same chart, same underlying data, a noticeably different story depending on which you choose.

Look again at that same sample dashboard: consistent teal coloring across every chart, consistent scale throughout, and a treemap where size itself does the sorting — the biggest manufacturer is simply the biggest rectangle on the page, no legend required. Every one of these is a small, deliberate storytelling decision, made on purpose rather than a Power BI default left untouched.

If this becomes a genuine interest, Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, Alberto Cairo, and Edward Tufte are all worth an afternoon of your time. Last lesson of the chapter: putting everything from these five lessons together into one professional executive dashboard, start to finish.
